Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The Guardian View image in fullscreen The former Conservative minister Ann Widdecombe was found dead at her home in Devon on 9 July. Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The Guardian UK news Widdecombe murder police reopen inquiry into alleged attempt to firebomb Farage’s home Watchdog examines handling of an incident last year that was treated as an attempted burglary Donna Ferguson and Nadeem Badshah Sat 8 Aug 2026 04.59 EDT First published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 18.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Counter-terrorism police investigating the death of Ann Widdecombe have reopened an inquiry into an incident last year, in which Nigel Farage’s home was allegedly firebombed. During the incident in April 2025, a lit incendiary device was pushed through the Reform UK leader’s letterbox, according to reports. Police did not identify any suspects during their investigation of the incident at the time, which was treated as an attempted burglary, and so the investigation was closed, pending any new lines of inquiry. Since the case was reopened, CTP London said it had identified a line of inquiry “which may have been relevant” but was “not identified and pursued by [counter-terrorism police] at the time”. The police watchdog said it was now investigating the conduct of a CTP London staff member over allegations that they “failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry”. Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism policing, said: “As part of the ongoing investigation led by counter-terrorism policing south-east into the murder of Ann Widdecombe, officers have reopened an investigation into an incident reported to police last year.” CTP London made a “mandatory conduct referral” to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) on Friday. A spokesperson for the IOPC said: “We can confirm that the IOPC has decided to independently investigate the conduct of a counter-terrorism policing London staff member following a referral received earlier today. “The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025. Counter-terrorism policing London has been notified of our decision, and no further information is available at this early stage.” Widdecombe, 78, a Reform UK spokesperson and former Conservative minister, was found dead on 9 July at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries. Last month, a 28-year-old man was charged with the former MP’s murder. Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July. He was also arrested on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism but has not been charged with this offence. Devon and Cornwall police initially arrested a 26-year-old man from Newton Abbot in Devon, but later released him and said he was no longer part of the investigation. Widdecombe served as Conservative MP for Maidstone, Kent, for 23 years. She subsequently represented south-west England as a member of the European parliament for the Brexit party and in 2023 joined Reform UK . Moscow reportedly sees further escalation as one of its few remaining ways to pursue its military aims. by Kyiv Post | Aug. 26, 2026, 11:03 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied A State Emergency Service (SES) rescuer cleans up after a Russian strike in the Kyiv region, Aug. 21. (Photo by State Emergency Service/Facebook) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Russia is preparing to escalate attacks on Kyiv, including the center of the capital, after reportedly concluding that peace negotiations have “reached a dead end.” According to Bloomberg , citing anonymous sources close to the Kremlin, Moscow is also considering intensifying conventional ballistic missiles attacks on other infrastructure targets across Ukraine. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . According to the sources, all attempts at negotiations have effectively collapsed, leaving Ukraine and Russia back at square one. NATO involvement Moscow increasingly sees Ukrainian strikes as attacks by NATO, because alliance members are supplying Kyiv with weapons and intelligence, Bloomberg’s sources said. “The current stage of hostilities isn’t the peak of military escalation,” according to the sources. Advertisement Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs said on June 6 that NATO must remain prepared for worst-case scenarios , describing Russia as dangerous and unpredictable and arguing that Russia’s next move was hard to predict. Meanwhile, EU countries on NATO’s eastern flank, including the Baltic states, are increasingly preparing for the possibility of Ukraine’s war spilling over onto their territory. Concerns have grown as drones have repeatedly violated the airspace of countries such as Romania , Poland , and Moldova , while Russia itself continues to prepare its youth for a conflict with NATO by 2030. Russian hybrid threats and cyberattacks have also increased in the past months. Other Topics of Interest Belarus Builds Military Rail Link Near Ukraine Border Ukraine’s border guards say no Russian or Belarusian force buildup has been detected near the frontier, despite the construction. Moscow sees very few alternatives Bloomberg’s sources said that Russian President Vladimir Putin was unlikely to end the war because of EU-imposed sanctions or Ukrainian attacks on critical oil , energy infrastructure and logistics networks . Four people close to the Kremlin said Russia now sees few alternatives to further escalation as it seeks to achieve its military objectives. According to Bloomberg, Russian authorities are hoping that a visit by US Special Envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff could bring new proposals, though expectations for a diplomatic breakthrough during the visit remain low. Advertisement Russia may be considering a nuclear option A growing number of Russian officials now believe Putin could eventually opt to use tactical nuclear weapons as a last resort in Ukraine. “An extreme response is viewed as possible because the only outcome worse than continuing the war for Putin would be losing it,” Bloomberg reported, adding that there is currently no indication that Russia is preparing to use the weapons. CIA chief visits Moscow The warning that Russia may escalate strikes on Ukraine comes as CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow on Tuesday, Aug. 25, after flying from Riga. Flight-tracking data indicated that the C-17 Globemaster III is a military transport aircraft first arrived in Riga on Sunday, Aug. 23, after departing from Camp Springs, Maryland, home to Andrews Air Force Base . “We have no information about this,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said when asked about the aircraft, adding that Russia was not planning meetings with the US administration. According to Peskov, Putin and Ratcliffe did not meet . The Kremlin later confirmed the visit, saying there had been “talks between the intelligence services.” Advertisement Axios , citing two anonymous US officials, reported that Washington had informed Kyiv ahead of the visit that a high-level US delegation was traveling to Moscow and had asked Ukraine to refrain from strikes on the Russian capital. While the purpose of the trip remains unclear, analysts suggest Ratcliffe’s meeting with Russian intelligence may have been related to the war in Ukraine, broader security concerns, or even the US-Iran conflict. On the same day as Ratcliffe’s visit, Putin signed three undisclosed decrees . The decrees, numbered 605, 606 and 607, were signed but not published, leaving their contents unknown. US President Donald Trump said Wednesday, Aug. 26, that Ratcliffe’s trip to Moscow could produce results as Washington seeks to end Russia’s war against Ukraine.“We would like to see the Ukraine war end,” Trump said, adding that his administration was “working very hard to get that war ended.” “Something may come out of it,” he continued. https://ecfr.eu/article/talk-is-cheap-eu.text: US secretary of state Marco Rubio described NATO’s July gathering in Ankara, two months before it convened, as “one of the more important leaders’ summits in [its] history.” The summit confirmed that Europeans have accepted America’s expectation that they do more for their own security. The Ankara declaration recognised that “European allies and Canada, working together with the United States, are assuming greater responsibility for the alliance’s defence.” Accepting that shift is one thing; paying for it is another. For European policymakers the question is now fiscal. It turns on what Europe is willing to pay for. And for the EU’s frugal members, that means rethinking what they treat as strategic. Getting defence into the budget According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies, replacing US military capabilities in Europe could require around $1tn (about €900bn) in extra investment. NATO’s new target to invest 5% of GDP in defence similarly implies a sustained increase in European defence spending over the coming decade. Together they suggest that defence is no longer crisis spending but a permanent claim on European budgets. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the EU has found money for defence, but always as extraordinary spending. The European Defence Fund and SAFE (Security Action for Europe, a loan scheme for joint arms purchases), for example, sit outside the ordinary budget. Such instruments expire; the challenge is to embed this spending into the EU’s regular budget. Winning defence a permanent line in it makes negotiations over the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) far more than another exercise in budgetary bargaining. The MFF is the EU’s seven-year budget—and where any pledge on defence would have to show up in funds. The commission’s proposal for 2028–34 reflects such a commitment. It allocates €131bn to defence and space, roughly five times the current level, and puts security among the EU’s central priorities. Out of the negotiating box Commission proposals rarely emerge intact from negotiation, and early signs suggest this pattern may repeat itself. Commission proposals rarely emerge intact from negotiation, however, and early signs suggest this pattern may repeat itself. Cyprus, which held the presidency until the end of June, left a negotiating box on how to structure the next MFF that envisioned reductions in defence and security while protecting cohesion policy and the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP). The box is the presidency’s draft compromise, the text the final deal is built from. The Irish presidency has opened with a strong focus on competitiveness and security, but Ireland leans heavily on farming too. Budget negotiations are shaped by coalitions that defend long-established spending. The 16 member states of the “Friends of Cohesion” group, Spain, Italy and Poland among them, want robust funding for cohesion policy and agriculture, while frugal member states, such as Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden, are reluctant to expand the overall size of the EU budget. Defence enters as a comparative newcomer against policies with decades of institutional backing and organised constituencies behind them. Germany’s position illustrates this dilemma. In a parliamentary inquiry, Alliance 90/The Greens asked the federal government how the EU can square four things at once: from 2028 it will need to start repaying NextGenerationEU, the €637bn joint borrowing agreed as a one-off in 2020 to fund members’ recovery from covid-19; forgo new revenue of its own (levies it collects directly rather than cheques from national treasuries); hold its budget roughly the same size; and still strengthen competitiveness, security and defence. The chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has repeatedly committed to the last three. The government answered that the EU could meet all three objectives by trimming across the whole budget. Yet such “horizontal cuts” only protect these priorities if all 27 members agree what to spare when deciding the cuts, and they are unlikely to agree. Other member states could favour different areas of the EU budget, cutting competitiveness or security harder than Germany intends. New financing for a new era The scale of investment required to deliver Europe’s defence transformation also exceeds what can realistically be financed through the MFF alone. While the seven-year budget can establish political priorities, provide long-term planning certainty and support common capability development, it cannot generate the sums required to finance Europe’s long-term defence. Hence the appeal of joint EU borrowing: debt raised by the commission against member-state guarantees, the model already used for NextGenerationEU and SAFE. NextGenerationEU demonstrated that the EU can raise substantial resources when confronted with an existential crisis such as the covid-19 pandemic. Europe’s security has changed just as fundamentally, which makes the case for borrowing together just as strong. If defence is a collective problem, leaving the bill to strained national budgets makes little sense. However, borrowing on that scale is politically out of reach: creditor states intend NextGenerationEU to stay an exception rather than a template. Something narrower—bonds (or comparable fiscal mechanisms) that fund defence alone or the technologies Europe cannot do without may prove necessary if the EU wants to match its strategic ambitions with adequate financial resources. Europe has accepted that it must carry more of its own defence. The MFF negotiations will show whether its budget can pay for it. With NATO entering a new era of European burden-sharing, the EU cannot afford a budget that reflects the priorities of a different geopolitical age. The world has moved on—it is time that frugal member states like Germany did so, too.

Photograph: Richard Drew/AP US markets Sharp drops for AI stocks overwhelm markets worldwide as oil prices jump Datacenter and chip costs fueled sharp decrease in AI sector although non-AI stocks still had a strong showing Associated Press Thu 22 Oct 2026 17.50 EDT Last modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 18.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The latest shudder for stocks in the AI industry pulled markets lower worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about the war with Iran . The S&P 500 fell 1.2% for its worst day since July, while the Nasdaq composite tumbled 2.6%. The weakness for tech stocks was so overwhelming that it masked strength for the rest of the US market, in which the majority of stocks actually rose. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11 points, or less than 0.1%. AI-related stocks have been swinging on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build datacenters and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that their prices shot too high following a years-long frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth. Oil prices jump to five-month high as attacks threaten global supply Read more Lam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 11.8%. Other big tech stocks likewise fell following quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets. Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7% after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, shedding tens of billions in market value, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it was creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses. Tesla fell 3.1% after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast. The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 4.4%. Because the chip giant is the largest company on Wall Street by total value, movements for its stock carry more weight on the S&P 500 than any other, and it was the single strongest force pulling the index lower. CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 10.1%. The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where indexes are full of players in the industry. South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5%, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3% and Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 2.7%. Also weighing on global stock markets was a jump in oil prices. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil leaped 4% to $113.17 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s shot up from less than $97 at the start of the month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal. In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1.4%. It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or US indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds. Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to TechScape A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives after newsletter promotion Worries about big government debt are weighing on almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong US economy and other factors, have pushed yields in the US bond market recently to their highest levels in decades. But US yields nevertheless fell sharply on Thursday in a signal that investors were buying US government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled. The yield on the 10-year treasury tumbled to 4.97% from 5.13% late on Wednesday and from more than 5.30% earlier this month. That’s a major move for the bond market. Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the US economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could signal that layoffs remain low across the country. That solid economy has helped US companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the US stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. Two out of every three stocks within the S&P 500 rose on Thursday, only to get drowned out by the drops for more influential tech stocks. Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses on Thursday. CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expected “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 5.6%. All told, the S&P 500 fell 93.74 points, to 7,663.43. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11.89, to 52,867.98, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 694.00, to 26,008.86. https://www.politico.eu/article/turkey-l.text: ATHENS — A controversial maritime border deal between Libya and Turkey has riled Greece, annoyed the European Union — and could intrude on Friday's EU leaders’ summit. Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis will raise the issue during the informal meeting of EU leaders in Dublin, according to a senior official in Athens who spoke on condition of being granted anonymity. The summit is supposed to focus on AI and Ukraine. The row centers on a Turkey-Libya agreement that claims a corridor in the eastern Mediterranean between Greece and Cyprus — waters Athens says fall within its exclusive economic zone and where the EU has backed energy and connectivity projects. Advertisement Advertisement “Greece has explicitly stated ... that in the event of any escalation, it will request sanctions and support from the European Union,” Greece’s Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis said last week in an interview with local TV. Despite being NATO allies, Greece and Turkey have quarreled over maritime boundaries and overlapping claims to their continental shelves. Athens fears Ankara could invoke the Libya deal to challenge offshore exploration south of Crete and the EU-funded undersea electricity cable linking Greece and Cyprus, turning both projects into flashpoints. Turkey signed the agreement in 2019 with Libya’s U.N.-backed government in Tripoli, and it was unanimously ratified by rival authorities in eastern Libya on Oct. 20. The EU immediately responded. "This agreement infringes upon the sovereign rights of third states, it does not comply with the Law of the Sea, and is null and void," said a joint statement on Oct. 20 from the heads of the European Commission and Council. Egypt also rejected the border pact, as did Bahrain, Cyprus (which has its own separate disputes with Turkey over Ankara's occupation of the northern part of the island since the 1970s), Israel and the United Arab Emirates. Advertisement Advertisement Turkish foreign ministry accused Brussels of adopting what it called the “maximalist and illegal” positions of Greece and Cyprus that were "detached from reality." “We expect them to respect the joint will of our country and Libya," Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan said during a recent Cabinet meeting. Mitsotakis raised the issue at last month's U.N. General Assembly, and Athens is now pressing the rest of the EU for stronger action. “There is no precedent for such a diagonal delimitation,” he said in New York, holding up a map to illustrate Greece’s position. “Geography cannot be rewritten … and sovereign rights cannot be erased by drawing arbitrary lines on a map.” The underwater border demarcation is part of a broader Turkish policy of stressing its sovereignty over coastal areas. Ankara aims to codify what it calls its Blue Homeland doctrine by year's end . The big test Greece and Cyprus warn that Turkey’s claims could be used to block strategic projects in the eastern Mediterranean. Advertisement Advertisement The EU's latest report on Turkey's stalled EU accession progress specifically referred to Ankara’s continued obstruction of a €1.9 billion electricity interconnection between Greece and Cyprus. The project was interrupted in 2024 amid a standoff between Athens and Ankara. Three months ago, French company Meridiam became the project’s majority shareholder. On Tuesday, a French vessel sailed from Heraklion, Greece, to start working on the project. Gerapetritis told a parliamentary committee last week that Athens is bracing for a Turkish reaction. Tension over the maritime border and the energy project comes as Turkey's already difficult ties with the EU — from protecting the car industry to Ankara's role in Black Sea security — come under greater pressure, noted Carnegie Europe Turkey analyst Marc Pierini. "In the eastern Mediterranean, several divergences over maritime borders have widened the gap between Turkey and EU governments," wrote Pierini. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6d7.text: Image source, Google Image caption, The BBC understands the man was based at Imjin Barracks in Gloucestershire By Amy Walker Published 10 November 2026 A soldier in the US Army has been arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia, British counter-terror police have said. The 41-year-old senior serviceman was arrested near Gloucester on Tuesday. Counter Terrorism Policing London said the man had been arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023. Section one of the Act relates to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while section three relates to assisting a foreign intelligence service. As part of the investigation, officers are carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire. The BBC understands the soldier was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire. The barracks serve as the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC) , a strategic operational base for the alliance. Counter Terrorism Policing said it was not linked to any other ongoing investigations. FBI director Kash Patel said in a statement: "This important arrest involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies." He added: "While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message â this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners." Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, from Counter Terrorism Policing London, described the arrest as "significant". "The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing," she said. The unnamed soldier is currently in custody at a London police station. He has been detained under the National Security Act 2023, allowing police to hold him without charge for up to 14 days. Brig Gen Sean Stinchon, commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command, said: "The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent. "I encourage anyone who thinks they've witnessed something suspicious to report it to their local counterintelligence office." Additional reporting by Daniel Sandford, UK correspondent.
